title: What Sound Is
bigQuestion: How does a shake in one place turn into a sound you hear somewhere else?

story.title: The Bass You Can Feel
story.kicker: At a summer block party, a soda can starts to shiver before you even hear the song.
paragraphs: It is a hot Saturday on a Chicago side street. Someone has set up two big speakers on a folding table. Kids are on the curb, grown-ups are at the grill, and a DJ is looking through a crate of records. A can of soda sits on the table next to the speakers.

The DJ drops the needle. The first thing you notice is not the music. It is the feeling. A low thump hits your chest. The table buzzes under your hand. The soda can shivers, and tiny rings dance across the top of the drink.

Walk to the end of the block and the song is still there, only softer. The high sounds, like the tss of the cymbals, seem to fade first. The deep thump carries farther. Nothing flew from the speaker to your ear. No wind blew. Yet something traveled a whole block and made your body feel it.

That something is sound. In this chapter you will find out what is really moving when a speaker plays, why some sounds are high and some are low, why some are loud and some are soft, and how your ear turns all of it into music.
story.think: The soda can shivered, but no one touched it. What do you think reached the can from the speaker?

lessons.title: Everything That Sounds Is Moving
lessons.mainIdea: Every sound starts with something vibrating, moving quickly back and forth.
reading: Put two fingers on the front of your throat and hum. You can feel a buzz. Now stop humming. The buzz stops too. That buzz is a *vibration*: a quick back-and-forth movement. Your vocal folds, two small flaps inside your throat, are shaking many times each second.

Every sound you have ever heard started this way. A drum skin shakes after the stick hits it. A guitar string shakes after it is plucked. A speaker has a cone that pushes out and pulls in. Even a clap makes your hands and the air between them shake for a moment.

Sometimes the shaking is too fast or too small to see. You can still find it. Sprinkle a little rice on a drum and tap the drum. The rice jumps. Put your hand on a speaker playing music. You feel it tremble. When the shaking stops, the sound stops. A *sound source* is anything that vibrates and starts a sound.

words.d: a quick back-and-forth movement
the object that vibrates and starts a sound, such as a drum skin or a speaker cone

look.title: The Silent Guitar
look.text: A student plucks a guitar string and hears a note. Then she presses her palm flat on the string. The note stops right away, even though the guitar is still right there.
look.prompt: Why did pressing the string stop the sound? Use the word vibration in your answer.

check.q: What do all sounds have in common at the start?
check.why: Every sound begins with a vibration, a quick back-and-forth movement.

check.q: Rice jumps on top of a drum when you tap it. What does this show?
choices: The rice is making the sound
Air is blowing out of the drum
check.why: The rice bounces because the drum skin under it is shaking back and forth.

check.q: You hum and feel a buzz in your throat. What is vibrating?
choices: The air in your lungs only
check.why: Two small flaps in your throat, the vocal folds, shake to make your voice.

try.en: Try it on the Drum Machine
try.es: Pruébalo en la caja de ritmos

lessons.title: A Chain of Pushes
lessons.mainIdea: Sound travels as a wave: each bit of air pushes the next bit, but the air itself stays close to home.
reading: When a speaker cone pushes out, it squeezes the air right in front of it. That squeezed air pushes on the air next to it. Then that air pushes the next air. The push passes along like a line of people bumping shoulders. This traveling push is a sound *wave*.

Here is the surprising part. The air near the speaker does not fly to your ear. Each bit of air moves forward a tiny bit, then springs back. What travels is the pattern of pushes, and the *energy* it carries. At the block party, no wind came from the speaker. Energy came.

A sound wave has places where air is squeezed together and places where it is spread apart. Scientists call the squeezed places *compressions*. The spread-out places are called rarefactions. A speaker making a steady note sends out compression, spread, compression, spread, over and over, as long as it keeps vibrating.

words.d: a repeating disturbance that carries energy from place to place
the ability to make something move or change
a place in a sound wave where the particles are squeezed close together

look.title: The Slinky on the Floor
look.text: Stretch a Slinky toy along the floor with a partner holding the far end. Give your end a quick shove forward. A bunched-up section races down the coils to your partner. Each coil only moves a little, then settles back.
look.prompt: What traveled down the Slinky? How is this like sound moving through air?

check.q: When you hear a speaker across the room, what reached your ear?
choices: Air that flew from the speaker to you
Energy carried by a chain of pushes in the air
check.why: The air only moves back and forth a little. The wave passes along the energy.

check.q: What is a compression in a sound wave?
choices: A place where there is no air
The loudest part of a song
A place where air is squeezed together
check.why: Compressions are squeezed places. The spread-out places between them are rarefactions.

check.q: A leaf floats on a pond as a ripple passes. What would you predict?
choices: It bobs up and down and stays near the same spot
It rides the ripple all the way to shore
check.why: Waves carry energy, not the material. The leaf, like the air in a sound wave, mostly stays put.

lessons.title: No Air, No Sound
lessons.mainIdea: Sound needs a medium, such as air, water or a solid, to travel through; in empty space there is no sound.
reading: If sound is a chain of pushes, it needs something to push. The material a wave travels through is called its *medium*. For the block party, the medium was air. But sound also travels through water and through solids like wood, metal and the ground.

In the 1600s, scientists built pumps that could pull most of the air out of a glass jar. Robert Boyle, working in England, put a ticking watch inside such a jar. As he pumped the air out, the ticking grew fainter. When he let air back in, the sound returned. With less medium, less sound got out.

Outer space is almost a perfect *vacuum*, a space with nearly no particles at all. So astronauts cannot talk to each other through empty space the way we talk in a room. They use radios. A radio sends light-like waves, which do not need a medium, and the receiver turns them back into sound inside the helmet.

words.d: the material a wave travels through, such as air, water or a solid
a space with almost no particles in it, not even air

look.title: The Watch in the Jar
look.text: Boyle reported that when he pumped the air out of a glass receiver holding a watch, the ticking could hardly be heard. When the air was let back in, the ticking could be heard again.
look.cite: Robert Boyle, New Experiments Physico-Mechanical, Touching the Spring of the Air, 1660
look.prompt: What did Boyle change in his test, and what did he observe? What does this tell us about sound?

check.q: Why can't sound travel through empty space?
choices: Space is too cold for sound
There are no particles to pass the pushes along
check.why: Sound is a chain of pushes. With no particles, there is nothing to push.

check.q: What did Boyle notice as he pumped air out of the jar?
check.why: Less air meant less medium to carry the sound, so it grew fainter.

check.q: Which of these is a medium sound can travel through?
check.why: Solids like steel carry sound well. A vacuum carries none.

sections.title: High and Low, Loud and Soft

lessons.title: Frequency Sets the Pitch
lessons.mainIdea: The faster something vibrates, the higher the pitch we hear.
reading: Pluck a thick, loose guitar string and you hear a low note. Pluck a thin, tight one and you hear a high note. The difference is speed. The thin string vibrates back and forth many more times each second. How high or low a sound seems is its *pitch*.

Scientists count vibrations per second. That count is the *frequency*. It is measured in *hertz*, written Hz. One hertz means one vibration each second. The A note that orchestras tune to is 440 Hz. The string making it moves back and forth 440 times in one second.

Double the frequency and you get the same note, only higher. Musicians call that jump an octave. The A above 440 Hz is 880 Hz. The A below is 220 Hz. On a drum machine, a deep kick drum is mostly low frequencies, and a tiny hi-hat is mostly very high ones.

words.d: how high or low a sound seems to a listener
how many vibrations or waves happen each second
the unit for frequency; 1 hertz (Hz) means one vibration per second

look.title: Notes Named A
look.prompt: What happens to the frequency each time you go up one A? Predict the frequency of A7.

check.q: A string vibrates faster than before. What happens to the pitch?
check.why: Faster vibration means higher frequency, and we hear a higher pitch.

check.q: What does 440 Hz mean?
check.why: Hertz counts vibrations per second.

check.q: An A note is 220 Hz. What is the A one octave higher?
check.why: Going up one octave doubles the frequency: 220 times 2 is 440.

lessons.title: Amplitude Sets the Loudness
lessons.mainIdea: A bigger vibration makes a wave with a bigger amplitude, and we hear it as louder.
reading: Tap a drum softly, then hit it hard. The pitch stays about the same, but the hard hit is louder. When you hit harder, the drum skin moves farther from its resting place. It squeezes the air more. The size of the vibration is its *amplitude*.

Loudness is how strong a sound seems. More amplitude means more energy in the wave, and it seems louder. Loudness is often measured in *decibels*, written dB. The scale is not a simple count. Every 10 dB step means the sound carries about ten times more energy.

So pitch and loudness are two different things. Pitch comes from how fast something vibrates. Loudness comes from how big the vibration is. A soft high note and a loud high note have the same frequency. On the oscilloscope, a louder sound draws taller waves. A higher sound draws waves packed closer together.

words.d: how far a vibration or wave moves from its resting place; bigger amplitude sounds louder
how strong a sound seems to a listener
a unit used to measure how loud a sound is, written dB

look.title: Two Taps on the Same Drum
look.text: You tap a snare drum gently with one finger. Then you hit it hard with a stick. Both hits make the same kind of snap. The second one makes the rice on the drum jump much higher.
look.prompt: Which one had the bigger amplitude? Did the frequency change much? How can you tell?

check.q: What changes when you hit a drum harder?
check.why: Hitting harder makes the skin move farther, which is a bigger amplitude and a louder sound.

check.q: On an oscilloscope, a louder sound looks like what?
check.why: Height on the screen shows amplitude. Loud sounds draw taller waves.

check.q: A sound goes from 60 dB to 70 dB. About how much more energy does it carry?
check.why: Each 10 dB step means about ten times more energy.

lessons.title: Wavelength and the Speed of Sound
lessons.mainIdea: Sound moves at a set speed in each material, and its wavelength is that speed divided by the frequency.
reading: Sound is fast, but not instant. In air at room temperature it travels about 343 meters each second. That is why you see lightning before you hear thunder. The light arrives almost at once. The sound takes about three seconds to cover each kilometer.

Sound moves even faster through water and faster still through steel. In solids and liquids the particles are packed close, so they pass each push along quickly. Put your ear on a long metal railing while a friend taps the far end. You may hear the tap through the metal first, then through the air.

The distance from one compression to the next is the *wavelength*. You can find it with a simple rule: wavelength equals speed divided by frequency. A 440 Hz note in air has a wavelength of about 343 divided by 440, or about 0.78 meters. Low bass notes have long waves, several meters long. That is part of why they carry around corners and through walls.

words.d: the distance from one compression to the next, or from one wave top to the next
how fast sound travels through a material; about 343 meters per second in room-temperature air

look.title: How Fast Sound Travels
look.cite: Standard reference values, rounded; wood varies by kind
look.prompt: Which material carries sound fastest? About how many times faster is steel than air?

check.q: You see lightning, then hear thunder three seconds later. Why the wait?
choices: Sound travels much more slowly than light
Sound goes slower when it is cold
Your ears work slower than your eyes
check.why: Light arrives almost instantly. Sound needs about three seconds per kilometer.

check.q: Through which material does sound travel fastest?
check.why: Tightly packed, stiff materials like steel pass the pushes along fastest.

check.q: A low note has a lower frequency than a high note. How do their wavelengths compare?
choices: The low note has a shorter wavelength
The low note has a longer wavelength
check.why: Wavelength is speed divided by frequency, so a smaller frequency gives a longer wave.

lessons.title: From Eardrum to Brain
lessons.mainIdea: The ear turns air vibrations into nerve signals, and the brain turns those signals into the sounds we notice.
reading: Your outer ear is shaped like a funnel. It gathers sound waves and sends them down a short tube to the *eardrum*, a thin skin stretched tight. When a sound wave arrives, the eardrum vibrates in the same pattern as the wave.

Behind the eardrum sit three tiny bones, the smallest in your body. They pass the vibration along and make it stronger. The last bone presses on the *cochlea*, a snail-shaped tube filled with fluid. Inside the cochlea are thousands of tiny hair cells. Different hair cells respond to different pitches.

When the hair cells bend, they send signals along a nerve to the brain. The brain does the rest. It tells a voice from a drum, finds the beat, and notices your name in a noisy room. Brains differ. Some people notice small sounds that others miss. Some people hear best with a quiet room or with headphones. Knowing what helps your own ears is useful science.

words.d: a thin, tight skin inside the ear that vibrates when sound waves reach it
a snail-shaped, fluid-filled part of the inner ear where hair cells turn vibrations into nerve signals
tiny cells in the cochlea that bend with vibrations and send signals to the brain

look.title: The Drum Inside Your Head
look.text: Your eardrum is a lot like the skin of a drum. But instead of being hit by a stick, it is pushed and pulled by the air. When a kick drum plays, your eardrum moves in and out in the same slow pattern as the speaker cone.
look.prompt: Follow one kick drum sound from the speaker cone to your brain. Name each step.

check.q: What does the eardrum do when a sound wave reaches it?
choices: It vibrates in the same pattern as the wave
It makes the sound louder by itself
It sends light to the brain
check.why: The eardrum copies the wave's pattern of pushes and pulls.

check.q: Where are the hair cells that turn vibrations into nerve signals?
check.why: The fluid-filled cochlea holds the hair cells.

check.q: Two students hear the same noisy room differently. What is the best explanation?
choices: One of them is not trying
Sound travels differently to each person
Brains and ears differ, and each person can learn what helps them hear
Only one of them has a cochlea
check.why: Hearing happens in the ear and the brain, and people's brains notice sounds in different ways.

lessons.title: The Sounds We Can Hear
lessons.mainIdea: People can hear roughly 20 to 20,000 hertz, and many animals hear sounds outside that range.
reading: Your ears do not hear every vibration. A young person with typical hearing hears from about 20 Hz, a very deep rumble, up to about 20,000 Hz, a thin whine. This span is your *hearing range*. As people get older, the top of the range usually drops.

Sounds too high for us are called *ultrasound*. Dogs can hear some of them, which is how a dog whistle works. Bats send out ultrasound and listen for echoes to find insects in the dark. Doctors use ultrasound to make pictures of the inside of the body.

Sounds too low for us are called infrasound. Elephants can use very low rumbles to stay in touch across long distances. Very low bass, near the bottom of our range, is often felt in the chest as much as it is heard. That is the thump you felt at the block party.

words.d: the span of frequencies a person or animal can hear
sound with a frequency too high for people to hear, above about 20,000 Hz

look.title: Top of the Hearing Range
look.cite: Rounded values from animal hearing studies; they vary by animal and by study
look.prompt: Which animal hears the highest sounds? Why might that help it?

check.q: About what is the typical hearing range for a young person?
check.why: Young people with typical hearing hear roughly 20 to 20,000 Hz.

check.q: A dog comes running at a whistle you cannot hear. What is the whistle probably making?
check.why: Dogs hear higher frequencies than people. A dog whistle uses sound above our range.

check.q: How do some bats find insects in the dark?
choices: They see in the dark with light from their eyes
They send out ultrasound and listen for echoes
They smell the insects from far away
They wait for insects to land on them
check.why: Bats use echoes of their own high calls to locate prey.

lessons.title: Loud Enough to Hurt
lessons.mainIdea: Very loud sound, or loud sound for a long time, can damage the hair cells in your ears for good.
reading: Hair cells in the cochlea are delicate. A very loud sound, or a loud sound that goes on for hours, can bend and break them. Once they are gone, the body does not grow new ones. This is called *noise-induced hearing loss*. It can happen without any pain.

The U.S. government's safety scientists say sound at 85 dB, about as loud as heavy city traffic, is safe for up to about eight hours a day. Each 3 dB louder cuts the safe time in half. At 100 dB, a level some headphones and concerts reach, the safe time is only about 15 minutes.

Protecting your hearing is simple. Turn it down. Take breaks. Step back from the speakers. Wear earplugs or ear defenders at loud events. Some people's ears are extra sensitive to noise, and ear defenders help them stay comfortable. That is a smart tool, just like sunglasses on a bright day.

words.d: a unit used to measure how loud a sound is, written dB
lasting damage to hearing caused by very loud sound or loud sound over a long time
earmuffs or plugs that make sound quieter before it reaches your ears

look.title: How Long Is Safe?
look.text: Exposure to sound should be kept below 85 dBA averaged over an eight-hour workday. For every 3 dB above that, the time a person can safely spend in the noise is cut in half.
look.cite: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), Recommended Exposure Limit for noise, 1998
look.prompt: If 85 dB is safe for 8 hours, how long is 88 dB safe? How long for 91 dB?

check.q: Why is noise-induced hearing loss so serious?
choices: Damaged hair cells do not grow back
check.why: Hair cells lost to loud sound are not replaced, so the loss lasts.

check.q: A sound is 88 dB. By the 3 dB rule, how long is it safe?
check.why: 85 dB is safe for about 8 hours. Each 3 dB louder cuts the time in half, so 88 dB is about 4 hours.

check.q: Which is a good way to protect hearing at a loud concert?
choices: Wear earplugs and take breaks away from the speakers
Stand right next to the speakers
Cover one ear only when it hurts
Turn up your headphones to drown it out
check.why: Earplugs and distance lower the level that reaches your cochlea.

lessons.title: Seeing Sound on a Screen
lessons.mainIdea: An oscilloscope draws a sound as a line over time, so you can see its frequency and its amplitude.
reading: A microphone works like an ear. Its thin plate vibrates with the sound, and it turns those vibrations into a changing electrical signal. An *oscilloscope* draws that signal as a line moving across a screen. Time runs from left to right. Up and down shows the push and pull of the air.

Now you can read a sound like a graph. Taller waves mean bigger amplitude, so a louder sound. Waves packed closer together mean higher frequency, so a higher pitch. The time for one full wave is the *period*. A 440 Hz note has a period of about 2.3 thousandths of a second.

Different sources draw different shapes. A flute draws a smooth, rounded wave. A buzzy synthesizer might draw a sawtooth. A hi-hat draws a fuzzy scribble, because it mixes many high frequencies at once. The shape of a wave is part of why a trumpet and a violin sound different, even when they play the same note.

words.d: a tool that draws a changing signal, such as a sound, as a line over time
the time it takes for one full wave to pass
the shape a sound makes when it is drawn over time

look.title: Two Lines on the Screen
look.text: On the oscilloscope, line A shows 4 smooth waves across the screen, each reaching halfway to the top. Line B shows 8 smooth waves across the same screen, each reaching only a quarter of the way up.
look.prompt: Which sound has the higher pitch? Which is louder? Explain what you looked at to decide.

check.q: On an oscilloscope, what does the left-to-right direction show?
check.why: Time runs across the screen. Up and down shows the air's push and pull.

check.q: Waves on the screen get closer together. What changed?
check.why: More waves in the same time means a higher frequency.

check.q: Why does a hi-hat look like a fuzzy scribble?
choices: It mixes many high frequencies at once
It is too quiet to draw
It makes only one low frequency
check.why: Cymbals and hi-hats make a noisy mix of many high frequencies, so the line looks rough.

review.why: Sound always begins with something moving quickly back and forth.

review.q: What moves from a speaker to your ear?
choices: Energy carried by a wave of pushes
review.why: The air mostly stays put; the pattern and its energy travel.

choices: There is no medium to carry the pushes
Sound only travels on Earth's surface
review.why: Sound needs particles to push. Space is nearly a vacuum.

review.q: Which change raises the pitch of a sound?
review.why: Pitch follows frequency. Faster vibration sounds higher.

review.q: Which change makes a sound louder?
review.why: Amplitude, the size of the vibration, sets loudness.

review.q: About how fast does sound travel in room-temperature air?
review.why: 343 m/s is the standard value for room-temperature air.

review.q: Which part of the ear holds the hair cells?
review.why: Hair cells in the fluid-filled cochlea turn vibrations into nerve signals.

review.q: A 10 dB rise means about how much more sound energy?
review.why: Every 10 dB step is about ten times the energy.
